title: The Three Begettings of the Flesh and the Two Names of the Pure
arc: The teaching classifies all fleshly life under three modes of begetting — by sexual joining, by the fall of the abortions, and by self-molding from the ground — and traces each mode back to its corresponding enthumesis; then, having shown how Hyle paints herself into every form of flesh, it explains the names "virgin" and "continent" at four ascending registers, ending with the New Man who has stripped himself of Sin.
reading:
This chapter teaches that everything the eye calls "flesh" — cattle, beasts, trees, plants, and human bodies — comes into being by one of three modes of begetting, and that these three modes are not biological curiosities but three discrete ways the corrupt matrix (Hyle's enthumesis) extrudes herself into the natural mind. The teaching first names the three: those begotten from one another (ordinary generation), those begotten in the abortions (the fallen offspring of the archons, falsities-from-evil cast down out of heaven), and those that mold themselves alone (self-generative growth from the earth). The "cattle and the rest of the creatures of the earth" exist accordingly in three likenesses, and even their nourishment is structured threefold to match the three modes of their begetting. The point is correspondential: the natural cosmos as we see it is the outer print of an inner structure of disordered desire, and what looks like merely vegetal or animal life is in fact the enthumesis of death taking shape at three discrete levels of the natural.

The teaching then unfolds the same threefold pattern through the trees. The first kind sprouted at the original word "Sprout up as grass!" — these are the bitter trees, the thornbushes and brambles of the dark land, in which the hidden enthumesis lodged inside the flesh-eating archons was planted as grass at the time when the powers were still in their substance. The second kind, molded by the same enthumesis when she came down out of the powers that eat flesh and grass, are trees that yield no nourishment at all: their fruit is reckoned neither as food nor as fodder, because the falsity that shaped them produces only sterile works. The third kind is that which Sin himself, descending from the [archons], planted in the earth according to his own counsel and teaching, so that the tree sprouted "in various likenesses and in various forms" — these are the trees that, when cut, sprout again from the root and bear fruit, because the enthumesis is seated in their root and bosom; others, where she is seated in the branches, regrow only when their branches are replanted; others, where the counsel is placed in the seed, grow only through their stock and seed. The whole botanical taxonomy is a precise correspondence: where the corrupt enthumesis lodges within a form determines how that form propagates, persists, or dies. Hyle is the painter, and every persistent form of fallen life is one of her paintings.

Having shown how the enthumesis of death generates flesh at every register, the teaching turns to its opposite — to what is gathered out of the flesh — and asks what is meant by the two names "virgin" (parthenos) and "continent" (enkratēs). The answer is given at four ascending registers, each register naming the same purity at a different degree. At the celestial register, the "virgin" is the sign of the entire Light in the mystery of the Aeons of the Greatness — the Light that has never tasted death, never come down to the war of the Enemy; uncorrupted reception in its primal state. The "continent" at this register is the mystery of the Light that did come down, was mingled and defiled in bodies, but went back up to the Light — divine truth that passed through the war and was raised. At the next register, the "virgin" is the Light chosen out from all the creatures and stood firm in the icon of the Ambassador and the icon of the gods — the purity that has emerged whole through the cosmic combat. The "continent" is the remainder of that Light still left behind in the one who was purified: part of it goes upward, part still falls downward through metensomatosis into the molding of further flesh, where it is again chosen out, becomes a holy one, and is named "continent." At the third register, the "virgin" is the Mind of Light that comes and bears the icons of the elect — illumined understanding clothing the chosen souls — and the "continent" is the New Man, chosen out from the Old Man, who purifies himself and strips himself naked of the Sin joined with him. At the lowest, ultimate register, the "virgin in the flesh" is a man who has never joined himself to a woman, never defiled himself in intercourse; the "continent" is the man who had a wife in the cosmos and afterwards purified himself from her and left her behind.

Read as one arc, the teaching moves from the cosmological floor to the celestial summit. It begins by exposing every form of natural life as a printing of Hyle's enthumesis at three discrete depths — root, branch, seed; abortions, mutual generation, self-molding — so that the reader sees the flesh itself as the painted body of corrupt desire. Then it lifts the same threefold/fourfold structure into its redemptive counterpart: at every level where Hyle has stamped her likeness, there is a corresponding station of purity — celestial Light untouched, descending Light that was mingled and returned, the Mind of Light bearing the elect, and the regenerate person in the body who has stripped off Sin. "Virgin" everywhere names what was never mingled; "continent" everywhere names what was mingled and has been chosen out and purified. The final fragments — the "true somatic dragon," "pneumatic," and "the dragon is the teaching of the flesh" — close the chapter by reasserting that the body, considered as flesh apart from this purifying choice, is still the dragon: the proprium in serpentine form. The whole teaching is therefore a sustained correspondential reading of natural generation: every begetting of flesh is the enthumesis painting herself, and every regeneration is the Light, in one of its four stations, being chosen out of her painting and stood firm in its own icon.
